domains.intro: The workspace is sliced vertically: every domain (a part of the app) owns its libraries, split into layers by what they do. Folders follow libs//-; libs/shared holds what several domains use. Generated from the Nx project graph.

api.text: The GraphQL schema and resolvers (@cv/api), answered in the browser for now.

data-access.text: A root signal store (NgRx Signals) that loads once and is shared app-wide. Internally a service runs a typed GraphQL query and a mapper turns the generated API types into hand-written frontend types.

feature.text: A routed page. Injects a store and renders its signals.

itcss.intro: The global styles in apps/cv/src/styles follow ITCSS (Inverted Triangle CSS), the way I learned it at SEM&BIO. Every layer is a folder, imported in order: broad rules with a low specificity first, narrow and specific ones last, so a later layer wins without specificity fights. Component styles stay encapsulated in Angular; the layers only hold what is truly global.
itcss.layer-texts: Variables and font definitions: typography, spacing, breakpoints and the Icomoon font.||Mixins and functions. They output no CSS until another layer uses them.||Third-party styles, high in the stack so the layers below can override them: the Angular Material theme, its palettes and overrides.||Bare HTML elements without a class: html, body, the scrollbar.||Layout patterns that arrange rather than decorate, shared by every page.||Self-contained pieces of UI. Nearly empty here: Angular components carry their own encapsulated styles.||Components that are too specific to reuse, like one particular header.||Extra specificity for one context, like .c-accordion.s-homepage. Kept nearly empty on purpose.||Single-purpose helpers that always win, the only layer where !important is allowed, like the accessibility and font classes.

state.intro: Every data-access library has an NgRx Signal Store: the Redux idea of one read-only source of truth, built on Angular signals instead of actions and reducers. Components never fetch data themselves.
state.steps: A service loads the data with httpResource and maps the API types to frontend types.||The store keeps it as state (withLinkedState), so it shows in the Redux DevTools, and adds a few methods (withMethods).||The page reads the signals, and Angular only updates what changed.

lib.intro: The opposite approach, for comparison: the component ships with this app instead of being loaded from another deployment.
lib.steps: MacWindow lives in this repository, in packages/mac-window.||It is published to npm as @axel-pauwels/mac-window.||This app installs it and bundles it at build time, so nothing is loaded at runtime.||It also ships as the web component (@axel-pauwels/mac-window/element), for any framework.
lib.subtitle: Bundled at build time, from this repository
lib.title: Component library: <lib-mac-window>

mfe.intro: A separate Angular app with its own repository and deployment. This app does not contain its code: it is loaded in the browser, when this page opens.
mfe.steps: At startup, initFederation() reads federation.manifest.json, which maps the name cv-mfe to the remote’s remoteEntry.json.||Here, Wrapper (@cv/shared-ui-federation) calls loadRemoteModule('cv-mfe', './web-components').||That module registers the custom element (Angular Elements), and the wrapper adds it to the page.||Angular and RxJS are shared with this app as singletons (Native Federation), so they are downloaded once.
mfe.subtitle: Loaded at runtime, from its own deployment
mfe.title: Micro-frontend: <cv-mfe>

branch.steps: It creates release/x.y.z from the green commit, with one commit that sets the version in package.json and package-lock.json.||Before pushing, it checks that both files carry the new version and that nothing else changed.||It opens the pull request into main, where GitHub checks the branch name, the version and CI, and deploys a preview.||Fixes found later go on develop; it opens a pull request from develop into the release branch, so I can review them first.
branch.subtitle: One version, everywhere
branch.title: Release branch and pull request

intro.rules: When something is unclear, such as a merge conflict or a failing check without an obvious cause, it stops and asks instead of guessing.||The decisions stay mine: it never picks the version, never merges a pull request and never pushes to main.||It follows the same rules as my release script and the checks on GitHub, so every step still works by hand too.
intro.subtitle: Plain-language instructions, checked into the repository
intro.text: My release process is written down as a Claude Code skill: a file in this repository (.claude/skills/release-flow/SKILL.md) that tells Claude, step by step, how this site is released. I say "push develop", "release" or "the release is merged", and Claude does the work with git and the GitHub CLI.
intro.title: A Claude Code skill runs my releases

merge.steps: I merge the release pull request myself, with a merge commit.||GitHub Actions tags the merge commit x.y.z, creates the GitHub release and deploys the site live.||Claude checks that the tag, the GitHub release and the version on main all match.||It pulls main locally and merges it into develop, so the next release starts from the released version. It asks before pushing.
merge.subtitle: Back in step, locally too
merge.title: Merge, tag and sync

push.steps: It pushes develop as is, skipping the release question of the pre-push hook.||It follows the GitHub Actions run: formatting, lint, unit tests, build, type check and end-to-end tests.||When a check fails, it reads the log, reproduces the failure locally with Nx, fixes it on develop, commits and pushes again.||After three rounds that are still red, or for problems outside the code (secrets, runners, outages), it stops and reports what it tried.
push.subtitle: Until every check is green
push.title: Push and fix develop

version.bumps: Major: breaking for visitors, such as a redesign or removed pages and links.||Minor: something new and visible, such as a page, a section or a language.||Patch: only fixes and improvements nobody sees.
version.intro: It compares develop with the latest release tag, both the commit messages and the actual changes, and recommends a version:
version.nothing: It only proposes; I choose. When nothing visible changed, it says so and asks whether a release is worth it.
version.subtitle: major.minor.patch
version.title: Choose the version
